title: Pooling Layers: Downsampling 🏊
description: Max pooling, average pooling, and why we shrink feature maps.

slides.title: Why Downsample? 📉
slides.content:
# Pooling Reduces Spatial Size

- Decreases computational load for deeper layers.
- Provides slight translation invariance (small shifts don't change output).
- Enlarges the receptive field of subsequent layers.

Most common: **Max Pooling** (take the maximum value in a window).

slides.title: Max Pooling in Keras
slides.content: Typically 2×2 window, stride 2 – halves the size.
slides.codeSnippet:
from tensorflow.keras.layers import MaxPooling2D

pool = MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2,2), strides=2)
# Input shape (batch, 28,28,32) → output (batch, 14,14,32)

quizData.question: After a MaxPooling2D(2,2) layer, the feature map size will:
quizData.explanation: A 2×2 pooling with stride 2 reduces each spatial dimension by a factor of 2.

slides.title: Max Pooling vs Average Pooling 🆚
slides.content:
# Max Pooling
Takes the maximum value in each window. Retains strong activations, adds non‑linearity.

# Average Pooling
Takes the mean. Smoother, but less common in modern CNNs.

# Global Pooling
`GlobalAveragePooling2D` reduces each feature map to a single number – often used before the final classifier.

slides.title: Global Pooling Example
slides.content: Often replaces a Flatten layer, reducing parameters.
slides.codeSnippet:
from tensorflow.keras.layers import GlobalAveragePooling2D

gap = GlobalAveragePooling2D()
# Input (batch, 7,7,64) → output (batch, 64)

slides.title: When to Use Pooling 🕹️
slides.content: Stack pattern: Conv2D → ReLU → Pool2D. Repeat several times, then Flatten/GlobalPool → Dense → output. Pooling is optional; some architectures use stride=2 convolutions instead.
